title: Getting Started with Burn
excerpt: Learn how to build and train your first neural network using Burn, the Rust deep learning framework designed for performance and flexibility.
body_md:
# Getting Started with Burn

Burn is a comprehensive deep learning framework built in Rust that prioritizes flexibility, performance, and ease of use.

## Installation

Add Burn to your `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
burn = "0.14"
burn-ndarray = "0.14"
```

## Your First Model

```rust
use burn::prelude::*;
use burn::nn;

#[derive(Module, Debug)]
pub struct MnistModel<B: Backend> {
    linear1: nn::Linear<B>,
    linear2: nn::Linear<B>,
    activation: nn::Relu,
}
```

## Training Loop

Burn provides a built-in `Learner` that handles training with metrics, logging, and checkpointing out of the box.

## Next Steps

- Explore the Burn book for advanced topics
- Try different backends (wgpu, tch, candle)
- Build a real project with Burn

title: Building an AI Agent with Rig
excerpt: Build a fully functional AI agent in Rust using the Rig framework — from a simple chatbot to tool-calling agents and RAG-powered assistants, with complete working code examples.

pages.title: Introduction & Setup
pages.body_md:
[Rig](https://rig.rs) is a Rust framework for building LLM-powered applications. It provides a unified interface across 20+ model providers, type-safe tool definitions, and built-in support for RAG — all with minimal boilerplate.

In this tutorial, you'll build three progressively more complex agents:

1. A simple conversational agent
2. An agent with custom tools it can call autonomously
3. A RAG-powered agent that answers questions from your own documents

> **Prerequisites:** Rust 1.75+, an OpenAI API key (or any supported provider), and basic familiarity with async Rust.

## Project Setup

Create a new project and add the dependencies:

```bash
cargo new rig-agent
cd rig-agent
```

```toml
[dependencies]
rig-core = "0.36"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
anyhow = "1"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
```

Set your API key:

```bash
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
```

Rig supports many providers (OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and more). We'll use OpenAI here, but swapping providers is a one-line change.

## Your First Agent

Let's start with a simple agent that has a system prompt and can answer questions.

```rust
use rig::providers::openai;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    // Create a client from the OPENAI_API_KEY env var
    let client = openai::Client::from_env();

    // Build an agent with a system prompt
    let agent = client
        .agent("gpt-4o")
        .preamble(
            "You are a Rust programming expert. \
             Give concise, practical answers with code examples. \
             Always explain *why* something works, not just *how*."
        )
        .temperature(0.7)
        .build();

    // Send a single prompt
    let response = agent
        .prompt("What's the difference between &str and String?")
        .await?;

    println!("{response}");
    Ok(())
}
```

Run it:

```bash
cargo run
```

### What's happening here?

- `openai::Client::from_env()` reads your API key from the environment
- `.agent("gpt-4o")` creates a builder targeting a specific model
- `.preamble(...)` sets the system prompt — this shapes the agent's personality and expertise
- `.temperature(0.7)` controls randomness (0.0 = deterministic, 1.0 = creative)
- `.prompt(...)` sends a one-shot message and returns the response

## Multi-turn Conversations

For back-and-forth conversations, use the `chat` method with message history:

```rust
use rig::providers::openai;
use rig::message::Message;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let client = openai::Client::from_env();

    let agent = client
        .agent("gpt-4o")
        .preamble("You are a helpful Rust tutor.")
        .build();

    // Build a conversation history
    let history = vec![
        Message::user("What is a trait?"),
    ];

    let response = agent.chat("Can you give me an example?", history).await?;
    println!("{response}");
    Ok(())
}
```

With the basics working, let's give the agent some real capabilities.

pages.title: Adding Tools
Building a Real-World Tool
RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
pages.body_md:
RAG lets your agent answer questions based on **your own data** by finding relevant documents and including them as context. Instead of relying only on the LLM's training data, the agent retrieves specific information at query time.

Rig makes this straightforward with its built-in vector store and embedding support.

## How RAG Works

1. **Index** — Your documents are converted to embeddings (numeric vectors) and stored
2. **Retrieve** — When a user asks a question, the question is also embedded, and the most similar documents are found
3. **Generate** — The retrieved documents are injected into the prompt as context, and the LLM generates a grounded answer

## Building a RAG Agent

No extra crates needed — Rig includes an in-memory vector store:

```rust
use rig::providers::openai;
use rig::vector_store::in_memory_store::InMemoryVectorStore;
use rig::embeddings::EmbeddingsBuilder;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let client = openai::Client::from_env();
    let embedding_model = client.embedding_model("text-embedding-3-small");

    // Create documents to search over
    let embeddings = EmbeddingsBuilder::new(embedding_model.clone())
        .simple_document(
            "ownership",
            "Rust's ownership system ensures memory safety without a garbage collector. \
             Each value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, \
             the value is dropped. Ownership can be transferred (moved) or \
             borrowed via references."
        )
        .simple_document(
            "lifetimes",
            "Lifetimes are Rust's way of ensuring references are valid. \
             The borrow checker uses lifetime annotations to verify that references \
             don't outlive the data they point to. Most lifetimes are inferred \
             automatically."
        )
        .simple_document(
            "traits",
            "Traits define shared behavior in Rust, similar to interfaces in other \
             languages. They can have default implementations, associated types, \
             and const values. Common traits include Display, Debug, Clone, \
             and Iterator."
        )
        .simple_document(
            "error-handling",
            "Rust uses Result<T, E> for recoverable errors and panic! for \
             unrecoverable ones. The ? operator propagates errors concisely. \
             Custom error types typically implement std::error::Error. \
             The thiserror and anyhow crates are popular helpers."
        )
        .build()
        .await?;

    // Store embeddings in an in-memory vector store
    let vector_store = InMemoryVectorStore::from_documents(embeddings);
    let index = vector_store.index(embedding_model);

    // Build a RAG agent — retrieves the top 2 most relevant documents
    let rag_agent = client
        .agent("gpt-4o")
        .preamble(
            "You are a Rust expert. Answer questions using the provided context. \
             If the context doesn't contain relevant information, say so."
        )
        .dynamic_context(2, index)
        .build();

    // Ask a question — the agent automatically retrieves relevant docs
    let response = rag_agent
        .prompt("How does Rust handle memory without garbage collection?")
        .await?;

    println!("{response}");
    Ok(())
}
```

### What `.dynamic_context(2, index)` does

When you call `.prompt(...)` on this agent:

1. The prompt is embedded using the same embedding model
2. The vector store finds the 2 most similar documents
3. Those documents are injected into the context alongside your preamble
4. The LLM generates an answer grounded in your actual data

The agent's response about ownership will cite the actual content you provided, rather than relying solely on training data.

## Production Vector Stores

The in-memory store is great for prototyping, but for production you'll want a persistent store. Rig supports:

| Store | Crate | Best for |
|-------|-------|----------|
| MongoDB | `rig-mongodb` | Full-stack apps already using Mongo |
| Qdrant | `rig-qdrant` | Dedicated vector search at scale |
| LanceDB | `rig-lancedb` | Embedded vector DB, no server needed |
| Neo4j | `rig-neo4j` | Graph + vector hybrid queries |
| SQLite | `rig-sqlite` | Lightweight, single-file storage |
| SurrealDB | `rig-surrealdb` | Multi-model database |

Swapping stores is seamless since they all implement the same `VectorStoreIndex` trait.
